#Agents #RL #Evals #RewardHacking
If your agent's reward comes from a script, the script is part of your threat model.

On October 11, 2026, arXiv published a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening.
The question it asks is whether today's model with scaled compute can automatically harden agent environments against reward hacking by potentially stronger future models.
The method first sets up an isolated verifier sandbox that agents cannot directly modify, then runs a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities.
Applied to Terminal Bench, KernelBench and SETA, it substantially reduced attack success, and the iterative design outperformed the static, non-iterative baseline.

On October 11, 2026, arXiv published a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening.
Agent environments are essential for large language model development, and they use programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards.
When those verifiers can be attacked, a cheating agent takes full credit without completing the intended task, which corrupts evaluation and misaligns training.
The framing is weak-to-strong: whether today's model, given scaled compute, can automatically harden agent environments to prevent potentially stronger future models from reward hacking.
The approach has two parts: an isolated verifier sandbox that agents cannot directly modify, and a hacker-fixer loop that finds and repairs the vulnerabilities the sandbox does not remove.
The sandbox closes the crudest route, where the agent edits the thing that grades it.
The loop then has to find the subtler ones, which is the part that does not finish.
Applied to Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, the loop substantially reduced attack success across these agent environments.
[source text withheld (the writer reproduced the page): sha256 15a73e558f4921b6d7e6f64926118cb39198f429ec93980cb9f4fd3686a142d5; 193 characters]
That is the comparison worth holding onto: a single hardening pass is the baseline the iterative version beats, so hardening behaves like a budget you spend rather than a patch you apply.
An earlier version of the hacker-fixer loop has been adopted by the official Terminal Bench repository as a way to audit exploits in its environments.
The authors state the standing condition plainly: as agent environments scale in numbers and difficulty, so must the repairing of exploitable verifiers.
Reduced attack success is measured against the attacks the loop itself generated, which is the usual limit of adversarial defence work and the reason the benchmark's own adoption carries weight.
The project page is at https://verifier-hardening.github.io/.

Training a GUI agent in a mocked ticketing app raised real-phone success from 28.8% to 48.1%
#Agents #RL #GUIAgents #OpenWeights
The open question for GUI agents has been whether cheap synthetic environments teach anything that survives on real hardware.
Here, RL in a mocked train-ticketing app transferred to its real-world counterpart, improving task success on a physical phone from 28.8% to 48.1%.
On October 14, 2026, arXiv published MAI-Gym, an open all-in-one platform that unifies GUI agent evaluation, data collection, and online RL training across mobile, computer, and web environments.
A shared rollout pipeline keeps agent behavior consistent across evaluation and training, and the platform supports ten established benchmarks and scales to 20,000 parallel environment instances.
It also synthesizes GUI applications and tasks automatically, including resettable mocked apps and coherent cross-app worlds with execution-validated task verifiers.
The trained model, MAI-Gym-9B, reached 78.4% on MobileWorld and 76.2% on OSWorld-Verified, state-of-the-art among open GUI agents under 10B parameters.
The motivating constraints remain the cost of interactive environments and the scarcity of realistic training tasks.
MAI-Gym releases the framework, synthesis skills, mocked apps, 2,000 verified tasks, and the model checkpoint.
If you are building a GUI agent, start by running your current one against the released tasks before writing any environment code of your own.
The mocked apps are the cheap part to reuse.

MAI-Gym unifies GUI agent evaluation, data collection, and online RL training across mobile, computer, and web environments through a shared rollout pipeline that keeps agent behavior consistent across evaluation and training.
It supports ten established benchmarks and scales to 20,000 parallel environment instances, and the 9B agent trained on it reached 78.4% on MobileWorld and 76.2% on OSWorld-Verified.
The platform addresses the cost of interactive environments and the scarcity of realistic training tasks, which are the constraints it was built against.
Copilot models were deprecated on October 19, 2026, and enterprise admins may have to enable the replacements
#AgenticCoding #Copilot #Deprecations
The deprecation covers most GitHub Copilot experiences, including Copilot Chat, inline edits, ask and agent modes, and code completions.
So a pinned model name in a script or integration breaks the same way the editor does, and on Enterprise the fix needs someone with policy access, not just you.
As of October 19, 2026, GitHub deprecated a set of models across most Copilot experiences, including Copilot Chat, inline edits, ask and agent modes, and code completions.
GitHub asks users to update their workflows and integrations to use supported models.
[source text withheld (the writer reproduced the page): sha256 b3802a8ad26170edf2d95e8d1b2633c01c4f4e462aae86a566155c882f56e6a5; 131 characters]

An administrator can verify availability by checking individual Copilot settings and confirming the policy is enabled for the specific model, after which it appears in the Copilot Chat model selector in VS Code and on github.com.
[source text withheld (the writer reproduced the page): sha256 f4d4beb52173bff645eaa497c10e43f92791d3d3574205870e2f9f9005e17d3d; 54 characters]
Grep your CI configuration, scripts and extension settings for hardcoded Copilot model names before your next build runs.
If a replacement does not appear in the Copilot Chat model selector in VS Code or on github.com, the policy has not been enabled for it.
That is an administrator's task, so raise it early rather than on the morning it blocks you.
Agentic autofix is generally available and reruns CodeQL before opening a pull request
#Agents #AgenticCoding #CodeSecurity
This is a shipped agent loop with a verifier inside it: it explores relevant files, proposes a fix, and reruns CodeQL to confirm the fix closes the alert before opening a pull request for review.
The gate is only as strong as what CodeQL counts as closed, which is why the review still lands on you.

Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts is now generally available to GitHub Code Security and GitHub Advanced Security customers on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.
[source text withheld (the writer reproduced the page): sha256 5ee69512e4fa055650d278ea0c3b4093c4fe217c2968291ab9a2b56c09147e45; 136 characters]
When enabled, it replaces the free Generate Fix option on individual code scanning alerts with an Assign to Copilot button.
It supports alerts on the repository's default branch only; alerts detected only on pull requests or other branches cannot be assigned to Copilot.
It also consumes AI Credits from your Code Security budget and GitHub Actions minutes.

An enterprise administrator must enable the new "Agentic autofix" policy in Advanced Security policies before an organization or repository administrator can turn it on in the Code Security settings for the organization or the repository.
Switch it on for one repository with a backlog of default-branch alerts, then read the validation steps in the first pull request before you widen it.
Agentic autofix consumes AI Credits from your Code Security budget and GitHub Actions minutes, and you can set SKU level budgets for Code Security AI credits.
Autofix trusts CodeQL to say an alert is closed, which is exactly the trust the verifier-hardening work attacks when it shows verifiers awarding full credit to agents that never did the task.
OpenAI models take the majority of Amp's tokens, with some users at 10 billion a week
#Agents #AgenticCoding #Tokens
One number here is worth keeping: OpenAI models account for the majority of tokens used in Amp, and Amp chooses and recommends models based on what works best for its users.
The rest is a vendor account of one customer, useful mainly as a picture of what token budgets do to how people use agents.
Amp describes building on GPT-6 Astra, Ultrafast, GPT-Live-1, and Sign in with ChatGPT.
Quinn describes some Amp users consuming 10 billion tokens a week, and says Amp launched its Sign in with ChatGPT integration partly to ease that constraint.
He says the integration gives users access to more tokens and OpenAI models, including GPT-6 Astra, which changes how willing they are to let an agent take on a larger task.

Amp also announced Puck, a conversational assistant built into Amp that helps users launch and manage other agents, with Calling Puck powered by GPT-Live-1 for real-time speech, including from a watch.
The claims are a single team's experience: Amp's own 20-person team uses agents including in marketing, and its Ultrafast testing with GPT-6 Astra is reported without measurements.
Copilot model policies can now be read and updated over the REST API
#Copilot #Platform #API
Model availability becomes configuration you can manage from code: REST endpoints now retrieve and update Copilot model policies for enterprises, enterprise teams, enterprise apps, and organizations.

GitHub added REST API support for retrieving and updating Copilot model policies for enterprises, enterprise teams, enterprise apps, and organizations.

Together, the endpoints are meant to make managing Copilot model availability across an enterprise easier.
GitHub points to its documentation on managing model availability and its REST API reference as the starting point.
Write a small script that reads your current policies and prints which models each organization may select.
Keep the output in version control so the next deprecation shows up as a diff rather than a support ticket.
The same model policies that an administrator may need to enable after the October 19 deprecation can now be read and updated through the REST API.
A mocked train-ticketing app taught an agent enough to move real-phone success from 28.8% to 48.1%.
Harness gains measured on a search set often failed to transfer to held-out tasks.

The week put two numbers next to one worry: overfitting and test-time scaling explained 54% and 14% of harness-evolution gains, while verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to agents that never did the task.

Against that, the practical work went the other way, with GitHub rerunning CodeQL to confirm a fix before opening a pull request and MAI-Gym holding agent behavior consistent across evaluation and training through a shared rollout pipeline.
Pick the agent change you are proudest of this month and measure it once more on tasks it was never tuned against.
Keep the number you get there, and throw the other one away.
